flashcards.q: List the five stages of the browser rendering pipeline in order.
flashcards.a: Parse (HTML->DOM, CSS->CSSOM) -> Render Tree -> Layout -> Paint -> Composite.

flashcards.q: Why is animating transform cheaper than animating top/left?
flashcards.a: transform on an already-promoted GPU layer skips layout and paint entirely; the compositor thread re-applies a matrix transform to the existing rasterized texture independent of the main thread. top/left are geometry properties that force layout, then paint, then composite, on the main thread.

flashcards.q: Difference between display:none and visibility:hidden in rendering cost?
flashcards.a: display:none removes the element from the render tree entirely -- zero layout/paint cost, no space occupied. visibility:hidden keeps it in the render tree, fully laid out and occupying space, but skips painting it.

flashcards.q: What is forced synchronous layout (layout thrashing) and how do you fix it?
flashcards.a: Reading a geometry property (offsetWidth, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop, getComputedStyle) right after writing a style forces the browser to synchronously flush pending layout to answer correctly. In a loop this turns 1 layout pass into N. Fix: batch all reads before all writes.

flashcards.q: What is the frame budget at 60Hz, 90Hz, and 120Hz?
Why use requestAnimationFrame instead of setTimeout for animations?
flashcards.a: requestAnimationFrame schedules its callback synced to the actual next paint at the display's real refresh rate. setTimeout has no relationship to the paint cycle and drifts relative to the true frame cadence, especially on non-60Hz displays.

flashcards.q: What does will-change do, and what is its real cost?
flashcards.a: Promotes the element to its own GPU-backed compositing layer in advance so the animation's first frame doesn't pay layer-creation cost. Cost: each layer consumes GPU memory (~width*height*4 bytes texture) plus compositing overhead -- applying it broadly or permanently causes 'layer explosion' and degrades performance, especially on GPU-constrained mobile devices.

The browser cannot safely paint until the CSSOM is complete, because any rule anywhere in an unparsed stylesheet could apply to already-parsed DOM nodes -- painting early risks a flash of incorrectly styled content that would then need to be redone.

flashcards.q: Why does an unmarked <script src> block HTML parsing, and what do defer/async change?
flashcards.a: A synchronous script could call document.write() and mutate the DOM being parsed, so parsing halts until it downloads and executes. defer downloads in parallel, executes after parsing completes, in document order. async downloads in parallel, executes whenever ready, no ordering guarantee.

flashcards.q: What is FLIP and when is it used?
flashcards.a: First-Last-Invert-Play: for genuinely layout-affecting animations (e.g. drag-to-reorder). Commit the real layout change once (synchronously), compute the visual delta between old and new position, then animate only that delta via transform -- getting compositor-cheap animation for something that is a real layout change.

flashcards.q: What does contain:paint/layout do and how does it differ from will-change?
flashcards.a: contain:layout/paint scopes layout or paint invalidation to the element's own subtree with a real guarantee (its internal layout can't affect outside, and vice versa), letting the engine skip checking outside. It's a lighter-weight invalidation-scoping tool distinct from will-change's GPU layer promotion.

flashcards.q: Name three triggers for an element getting its own GPU compositing layer.
flashcards.a: will-change: transform (or other compositor-eligible property), 3D transforms (transform3d/translateZ), <video>/<canvas> elements, an in-flight opacity animation, certain position:fixed cases.
